title: Millennials and Gen X Are Aging Faster Biologically Than Their Parents — and a Major Study Links It to Rising Cancer Rates
excerpt: A Nature Medicine analysis of over 150,000 people finds that recent generations show accelerated biological aging, which may help explain the surge in early-onset cancers — a trend with particular implications for South Asians.
body:
If you were born after 1965, your body may be aging faster than your parents' did at the same chronological age. And according to a landmark study published in *Nature Medicine* on July 1, that accelerated internal clock could help explain one of modern medicine's most troubling trends: why cancer is striking younger and younger adults.

The study, titled "Biological aging and generational shifts in early-onset cancer risk," analysed data from more than 150,000 participants in the UK Biobank and cross-validated its findings with over 10,000 individuals in the United States' All of Us Research Program. Its central finding is stark: people born in later decades show measurably faster biological aging — and that aging is linked to a higher risk of developing solid cancers before the age of 55.

## The Numbers That Should Worry You

Using PhenoAge — a well-established biological age calculator that estimates internal aging from blood biomarkers — the researchers found that people born between 1965 and 1974 had a 23% higher standardised age gap than those born between 1950 and 1954. In the American cohort, the gap was even more dramatic: individuals born between 1990 and 1999 showed a 92% higher biological aging marker than those born in the mid-1960s.

In plain terms, a 35-year-old today may have the biological profile of someone several years older by the standards of previous generations. And that internal wear shows up in cancer risk. Each standard-deviation increase in the PhenoAge gap was associated with an 8% higher likelihood of developing an early-onset cancer — even after adjusting for genetic predisposition.

## It's Not Just Systemic — It's Organ-Specific

The study went further by deploying organ-specific biological aging clocks built from proteomic data. The results were striking: accelerated immune tissue aging was linked to a 89% higher risk of early-onset lung cancer, while faster adipose (fat) tissue aging was tied to a 60% higher risk of early-onset colorectal cancer.

These associations held even after accounting for systemic aging, suggesting that specific organs can deteriorate at different rates — and that the organ that ages fastest may determine which cancer develops first.

## Why South Asians Should Pay Particular Attention

The diaspora implications are significant. South Asians already carry a disproportionate burden of metabolic disease — higher rates of insulin resistance, visceral fat accumulation, and cardiovascular events at younger ages compared to European populations. The MASALA study, the largest US longitudinal study of South Asian heart health, has consistently shown that these risks emerge earlier and at lower BMI thresholds.

The new biological aging data adds another layer to this picture. If metabolic dysfunction accelerates internal aging, and accelerated aging increases cancer risk, then the South Asian diaspora may face a compounding vulnerability that standard screening guidelines — designed for populations with slower biological aging — fail to capture.

Colorectal cancer, in particular, is rising sharply among younger adults globally. The American Cancer Society now recommends screening starting at age 45, down from 50. For South Asians with elevated metabolic markers, the new findings suggest that even 45 may not be early enough.

## What's Driving the Acceleration?

The study does not pinpoint a single cause, but the authors note that biological aging clocks likely capture the cumulative effect of environmental and lifestyle exposures — diet, pollution, sleep disruption, chronic stress, and metabolic dysfunction. A mediation analysis found that lifestyle factors only modestly explained the PhenoAge results, suggesting that exposures beyond individual behaviour — environmental chemicals, ultra-processed food systems, sedentary infrastructure — may play a role.

For NRIs navigating two food systems, two stress landscapes, and two healthcare paradigms, the message is practical: biological aging may be running faster than chronological aging, and standard age-based health milestones may need to be pulled forward.

## What You Can Do Now

The study is observational and its organ-specific findings are exploratory. Biological aging clocks are not yet clinical tools. But the researchers are clear about the direction: if validated, these clocks could eventually help doctors identify who is aging fastest — and who needs earlier screening, more aggressive prevention, or closer monitoring.

In the meantime, the evidence converges on a familiar but urgent prescription: regular metabolic screening (fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panels) starting in your 30s, colorectal cancer screening no later than 45, sustained physical activity, and a diet that prioritises fibre, whole foods, and anti-inflammatory nutrients over the ultra-processed convenience that has become a hallmark of modern diasporic life.

Your chronological age is a number. Your biological age, increasingly, is a warning.

*Source: Tian, R., Zong, X., Ren, D. et al. "Biological aging and generational shifts in early-onset cancer risk." Nature Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41591-026-04448-w*
